l1: Is the WDAC policy running in Audit mode or Enforced mode?
What is the exact file, driver, or script that is being blocked or reported?
Was this policy deployed via Group Policy, Intune (ApplicationControl CSP), or applied locally?
Did the block start after a policy change, an application update, or a new driver install?
Has this exact policy been tested successfully in Audit mode before being moved to Enforced?
l2: Is Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI) or Smart App Control also enabled alongside this WDAC policy?
Is this a single-policy (legacy, .p7b) or multiple-policy (base + supplemental, .cip) WDAC deployment?
Does the blocked file rely on a revoked or expired code-signing certificate with a lifetime signing EKU?
Is the Intelligent Security Graph (ISG) or a Managed Installer (MI) being used to authorize otherwise-unsigned files?

l1: Check Event Viewer > Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > CodeIntegrity > Operational for block events.
Confirm which policies are currently active under C:\Windows\System32\CodeIntegrity\CiPolicies\Active.
Check whether the policy is in Audit or Enforced mode by inspecting the policy XML's Audit Mode rule option.
Confirm the exact file path, publisher, and hash of the blocked file from the event details.
l2: Event ID 3076 = audit-mode block (would be blocked if enforced); Event ID 3077 = enforced-mode block (file was actually blocked) — confirm which one you're seeing.
Event ID 3033/3034 usually indicates a revoked or expired lifetime-signing certificate on the blocked file, not a policy misconfiguration.

If multiple policies appear active but only a default/unexpected one is enforcing, use wbemtest to browse the WMI Bridge (root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard) for stale or duplicate CI policy instances.
Run 'Get-SystemDriver' or review the merged policy XML to confirm which specific rule (publisher, hash, path, or FilePublisher) is matching — or failing to match — the blocked file.

l1: If testing, temporarily set the policy to Audit mode to confirm whether it is the cause before rolling back to Enforced.
Confirm the blocking file's digital signature is valid, current, and from a trusted publisher.
Re-deploy the policy and reboot to force a refresh if the device may be running a stale policy.
Check for a duplicate or conflicting default policy that may be taking precedence over the intended one.
Check whether HVCI (Memory Integrity) is enabled alongside WDAC, since an incompatible driver can be blocked by HVCI rather than the WDAC policy itself.
Confirm the policy was actually redeployed/refreshed after editing — a stale cached policy is a common cause of 'my change didn't take effect'.
l2: For a stale/duplicate policy taking precedence, use wbemtest to locate and delete the offending CI policy instance directly from the WMI Bridge, then reboot.
For a signature-expiry block (3033/3034), add rule option 'Enabled:Revoked Expired As Unsigned' along with rules (e.g. hash-based) that don't depend on the revoked/expired certificate.
For a legitimate new tool being blocked, add a supplemental policy rule (publisher, hash, or path) rather than disabling enforcement broadly.

Update the Microsoft recommended driver block rules (driversipolicy.p7b / a newer SiPolicy.p7b) if HVCI, Smart App Control, or S mode is blocking a specific vulnerable driver, and verify via the CodeIntegrity event log after refreshing.

l1: Record the exact CodeIntegrity event ID and blocked file path from Event Viewer.
Note whether the policy is in Audit or Enforced mode.
Confirm the deployment method — GPO, Intune, or local policy.
Note whether the block began after a specific policy or application change.
l2: Export the CodeIntegrity - Operational event log covering the block event(s).
Collect the deployed policy XML (or the merged policy) from C:\Windows\System32\CodeIntegrity\CiPolicies\Active.
If a signature issue is suspected, collect the blocked file's certificate chain and signing timestamp.
If a stale policy is suspected, collect the WMI Bridge CI policy instances via wbemtest for comparison against the intended deployment.

legitimate_app_blocked_in_enforced_mode.title: A legitimate, trusted application is blocked once policy moves to Enforced mode

steps.action: Confirm CodeIntegrity - Operational shows Event ID 3077 (enforced block) for the specific file
steps.expect: Confirms WDAC, not another control, is blocking the file

steps.action: Check the file's publisher, hash, and signing status against the active policy's rules
steps.expect: Identifies exactly which rule type (or its absence) is causing the block

steps.action: Add a supplemental policy rule (publisher, path, or hash) authorizing the specific application
steps.expect: Merged policy now includes an allow rule for the app

steps.action: Redeploy the updated policy and refresh (or reboot) the device
steps.expect: Application launches without a CodeIntegrity block

steps.action: Re-check CodeIntegrity - Operational for the application
steps.expect: No further 3077 block events for this application

stale_default_policy_overriding_custom_p.title: Device enforces the default built-in policy instead of the deployed custom policy

steps.action: Check CodeIntegrity - Operational events for a Policy ID that doesn't match the custom policy's expected ID
steps.expect: Confirms a different (often default) policy is actually enforcing

steps.action: Use wbemtest to browse the WMI Bridge (root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard) and list all CI policy instances
steps.expect: Identifies a duplicate or stale policy instance still present alongside the intended one

steps.action: Delete the offending stale policy instance directly from wbemtest
steps.expect: Only the intended policy instance remains
Policy re-evaluation picks up only the intended policy

steps.action: Re-check CodeIntegrity - Operational events for the expected Policy ID
steps.expect: Events now reference the correct, intended policy ID

hvci_incompatible_driver_blocks_boot.title: A driver incompatible with HVCI/Memory Integrity blocks boot or causes a crash

steps.action: Boot into Safe Mode or WinRE and check whether disabling Memory Integrity (Core Isolation) resolves the boot issue
steps.expect: Confirms HVCI/driver incompatibility as the cause rather than a broader boot failure

steps.action: Check the CodeIntegrity - Operational log and Microsoft's HVCI driver compatibility guidance for the specific incompatible driver
steps.expect: Identifies the exact driver that isn't HVCI-compatible

steps.action: Update the driver to an HVCI-compatible version from the vendor, or if unavailable, exempt/remove that specific driver rather than disabling HVCI fleet-wide
steps.expect: Compatible driver is in place, or the incompatible one is removed
Device boots normally with HVCI enabled and no further crashes

policy_change_not_taking_effect.title: An edited WDAC policy doesn't seem to take effect on the device

steps.action: Confirm the policy file's version/PolicyID was actually incremented and redeployed, not just edited locally
steps.expect: Confirms whether a genuinely new policy was pushed

steps.action: Check C:\Windows\System32\CodeIntegrity\CiPolicies\Active for the deployed policy's timestamp and compare against the intended version
steps.expect: Confirms whether the device actually received the updated policy file

steps.action: Redeploy via the correct channel (GPO/Intune/manual copy) and force a policy refresh or reboot, since some policy types require a restart to take effect
steps.expect: Updated policy file lands and is picked up

steps.action: Re-check the CiPolicies\Active timestamp and test the specific rule change
steps.expect: New policy is active and the intended rule change is enforced
